title: Direct sums and finite cohomological dimension
statement:
Let $n\ge1$, and let $f:X\to Y$ be a
quasi-compact and
quasi-separated morphism with $\kuncd(f)<\infty$.

1. **(1)** $Rf_*:D(X_{\Et},\kunZn)\to D(Y_{\Et},\kunZn)$ commutes with
set-indexed direct sums.
1. **(2)** If $X$ is a qcqs scheme with $\kuncd(X)<\infty$, then
$\RGamma(X_{\Et},-):D(X_{\Et},\kunZn)\to D(\kunZn)$ commutes with
set-indexed direct sums.

proof.text: Put $A=\mathbf Z/n\mathbf Z$. Every $A$-module sheaf is torsion as an abelian sheaf, since $n$ kills all sections. The natural higher-direct-image coefficient comparison identifies the underlying abelian sheaf of $R^qf_*M$ with $R^qf_*$ of the underlying sheaf. Thus $\kuncd(f)<\infty$ supplies $d\geq0$ with $R^qf_*M=0$ in the module category for all $q>d$. For a set-indexed family $(M_i)$ of module sheaves, write its sum as the filtered colimit of finite partial sums, indexed by finite subsets of the index set (including the empty subset). Module colimits have the underlying abelian colimits. Apply the filtered-colimit direct-image theorem to these torsion sheaves. Finite sums commute with $R^qf_*$ by additivity (take the finite sum of injective resolutions). Hence the canonical map $\bigoplus_iR^qf_*M_i\to R^qf_*(\bigoplus_iM_i)$ is an isomorphism for every $q\geq0$, including $q=0$. All maps are $A$-linear; exact faithful forgetting reflects their invertibility.

The categories of $A$-module sheaves on $X_{\mathrm{Et}}$ and $Y_{\mathrm{Et}}$ are Grothendieck abelian. Given arbitrary $E_i\in D(X_{\mathrm{Et}},A)$, choose representatives $K_i^\bullet$ and K-injective resolutions $K_i^\bullet\to I_i^\bullet$ with each $I_i^r$ injective. The termwise sum $L^\bullet=\bigoplus_i I_i^\bullet$ represents the coproduct $\bigoplus_i E_i$ by the Grothendieck derived-coproduct theorem. No common bound on the $E_i$ is imposed.

For an injective $J$, the resolution concentrated in degree zero computes $R^qf_*J$ by a complex concentrated in degree zero, so $R^qf_*J=0$ for $q>0$. In particular each $I_i^r$ is $f_*$-acyclic. Step 1 gives, for every $q>0$ and $r\in\mathbf Z$, $R^qf_*(L^r)\cong\bigoplus_iR^qf_*I_i^r=0$. Thus both $I_i^\bullet$ and $L^\bullet$ consist of $f_*$-acyclic objects. The module direct image is additive and left exact; its finite cohomological dimension was established in Step 1. The unbounded acyclic-complex theorem therefore represents $Rf_*E_i$ by $f_*I_i^\bullet$ and $Rf_*(\bigoplus_iE_i)$ by $f_*L^\bullet$. Its natural comparison identifies $Rf_*$ of each coprojection with the corresponding map of these complexes.

The $q=0$ case of Step 1 is a natural isomorphism $\bigoplus_i f_*I_i^r\cong f_*(\bigoplus_iI_i^r)$ for every degree $r$. Naturality with respect to the differentials makes these isomorphisms a complex isomorphism $\bigoplus_i f_*I_i^\bullet\cong f_*L^\bullet$, whose composite with the $i$th coprojection is $f_*$ of the $i$th coprojection into $L^\bullet$. Apply localization. Since the target sheaf category is Grothendieck abelian, the derived-coproduct theorem identifies the left complex with $\bigoplus_iRf_*E_i$. Step 3 identifies the right complex with $Rf_*(\bigoplus_iE_i)$ and identifies its legs. This proves that the canonical coproduct comparison is invertible, proving (1).

For (2), work directly with $F=\Gamma(X,-):\operatorname{Mod}(X_{\mathrm{Et}},A)\to\operatorname{Mod}(A)$, rather than identifying global sections with a scheme-theoretic structure morphism. This is additive because sections preserve addition of maps; it preserves kernels because module-sheaf kernels are sectionwise, so it is left exact. The cohomology coefficient comparison identifies the underlying group of $R^qF(M)$ with $H^q(X_{\mathrm{Et}},M_{\mathrm{ab}})$. Thus $\kuncd(X)<\infty$ supplies a uniform bound $d_X$ for $R^qF$ on all module sheaves. On the qcqs scheme $X$, cohomology commutes with filtered colimits, also for constant-ring module sheaves. For the filtered poset of finite subsets $J$ of the index set, put $M_J=\bigoplus_{i\in J}M_i$. Its colimit is $\bigoplus_iM_i$. A finite sum of injective resolutions is an injective resolution of the finite sum (finite biproducts of injectives are injective), and applying the additive functor $F$ and taking cohomology commutes with this finite sum. Consequently $R^qF(M_J)=\bigoplus_{i\in J}R^qF(M_i)$. Taking the filtered colimit of these equalities proves $R^qF(\bigoplus_iM_i)\cong\bigoplus_iR^qF(M_i)$ for all $q\geq0$. Here finite sums commute by additivity, and the filtered-colimit comparison is the canonical one.

Choose the complexes $I_i^\bullet$ and $L^\bullet$ as in Step 2 on $X$. For an injective sheaf $J$, its degree-zero injective resolution gives $R^qF(J)=0$ for $q>0$, so the terms $I_i^r$ are $F$-acyclic; the positive-degree comparisons of Step 5 imply that each $L^r=\bigoplus_iI_i^r$ is $F$-acyclic. The unbounded acyclic-complex theorem, using the bound $d_X$, represents $R\Gamma(X,E_i)$ by $\Gamma(X,I_i^\bullet)$ and $R\Gamma(X,\bigoplus_iE_i)$ by $\Gamma(X,L^\bullet)$, naturally on the coprojections. Write $\theta_r:\bigoplus_iF(I_i^r)\to F(L^r)$ for the degree-zero comparison of Step 5 and $\iota_i^r:I_i^r\to L^r$ for a coprojection. Then $\theta_r$ composed with the $i$th coprojection is $F(\iota_i^r)$. Since $d_L^r\iota_i^r=\iota_i^{r+1}d_i^r$, applying $F$ shows that $F(d_L^r)\theta_r=\theta_{r+1}(\bigoplus_iF(d_i^r))$, by equality on every coprojection. Thus the $\theta_r$ give a complex isomorphism $\bigoplus_i\Gamma(X,I_i^\bullet)\to\Gamma(X,L^\bullet)$ preserving all coprojections. Termwise sums of $A$-module complexes compute coproducts in $D(A)$. Therefore this isomorphism is exactly the canonical map $\bigoplus_iR\Gamma(X,E_i)\to R\Gamma(X,\bigoplus_iE_i)$, which proves (2). The argument also includes the empty family, whose sum and image are zero.
